## Abstract

Deep learning models learn patterns from training data. Biases and inconsistencies in this training data affect the model's ability to learn patterns that allow for correct classification of images. The deep learning models I have trained so far have peaked at 65.3% validation accuracy (agreement with the median score). Here I present the annotated CDA image dataset and show that the score annotations collected are inconsistent between scorers. I show that these scoring inconsistencies are not due to the method of image allocation to scorers, but may instead be due to differences in opinion comparing CDA images to the unclear scoring key. This in particular makes it challenging to distinguish between scores of adjacent classes. These scoring inconsistencies mean that score classes cannot be accurately distinguished by non-deep-learning clustering methods, and they limit the performance of the deep learning models. I propose some next steps to try to improve model performance by excluding annotation portions that negatively contribute to scoring agreement and by reconsidering scoring labels and model performance metrics.

\newpage

## Agroinfiltration assignment and scoring approach.

For each original agroinfiltration image, I estimated the number of CDAs by multiplying the number of leaves by the number of positions per leaf. These estimates were summed to give a total CDA count estimate. The images were evenly divided amongst the scorers using these estimates, in a way that each CDA was scored by three scorers (@tbl-allocations).

| Data subset (all equal in size) | Scorer1 | Scorer2 | Scorer3 |
|---------------------------------|---------|---------|---------|
| A                               | 1       | 2       | 3       |
| B                               | 2       | 3       | 4       |
| C                               | 3       | 4       | 5       |
| D                               | 4       | 5       | 6       |
| E                               | 5       | 6       | 7       |
| F                               | 6       | 7       | 8       |
| G                               | 7       | 8       | 9       |
| H                               | 8       | 9       | 1       |
| I                               | 9       | 1       | 2       |

: Staggered agroinfiltration image distribution pattern for CDAScorer score and coordinate collection. {#tbl-allocations}

The Banfield lab members used the package CDAScorer to collect score and coordinate data each CDA. This was done in two parts A and B. For part A there were 8 scorers and for part B 9, with 7 common to both parts. I manually checked that each collected annotation was correctly matched to the recorded row, column, and positions. I corrected mismatched bounding box annotations and excluded erroneous bounding box annotations, without changing any score annotations. Criteria for exclusion were bounding boxes a) not on a CDA, b) only partially covering a CDA, c) or over multiple CDAs, or d) double annotations from the same scorer (the first collected annotation was kept). I excluded any CDA with either just one annotation or two annotations with disagreeing scores.

\newpage

## CDAScorer was used to annotate a CDA image dataset.

The Banfield lab members recorded 18,881 score and coordinate annotations (@fig-allscores) from 6,336 CDAs. For each CDA, a median score was calculated. There was variability in scoring agreement between scores - For CDAs of score 0, the vast majority of scores were 0s. For intermediate CDAs of intermediate scores like 3, there was a much broader variability in scores collected.

![All 18,881 scores collected for the CDA dataset, faceted by the median score of the corresponding CDA. For each CDA index (X-axis), there are multiple scores (Y-axis) by different scorers. Faceted by median score.](all_scores.png){#fig-allscores}

Some scorers collected fewer annotations than others (@tbl-annotationsperscorer). Part A of the dataset contained orange CDAs as well as the typical yellow-green ones. These were included in the estimate used to allocated agroinfiltration images but were not annotated, which may explain differences in annotation numbers in part A of the dataset. In part B, there were no orange CDAs, which is reflected in the more even distribution of annotation counts. The difference in score counts between scorers could bias the model towards the patterns shown by those with more scores collected. Given the distribution of scores, we might expect the model to be biased against patterns from scorers 1, 5, and 7, who only scored one part of the dataset.

### Annotations by score

Across the combined dataset, some scores were collected more often than others (@tbl-scorecounts). CDAs with a median score of 0 represented 42.6% of the image dataset. All experiments included negative controls with an expected score of 0, which is likely to explain this imbalance.

| Score | Annotation Count | CDA Label Count (Median) | % of CDA Labels |
|-----------------|-----------------|-----------------|----------------------|
| 0     | 7,872            | 2,699        | 42.6                                 |
| 1     | 1,445            | 425          | 6.7                                  |
| 2     | 1,275            | 434          | 6.8                                  |
| 3     | 2,066            | 705          | 11.1                                 |
| 4     | 2,483            | 843          | 13.3                                 |
| 5     | 2008             | 701          | 11.1                                 |
| 6     | 1732             | 529          | 8.4                                  |

: Score counts. {#tbl-scorecounts}

The proportion of scores collected also differed between scorers (@fig-scoreprops), which could highlight scoring biases. Scorer 1 scored a lower proportion of 1s, 2s, 3s, and 4s than any other scorer, indicating they may favour extreme scores. Scorer 10 scored almost double as many 1s as the next highest, but as a consequence scored fewer 0s than almost all others.

![Proportion of scores collected by each scorer. "\[\]" represents missing scores.](score_proportions.png){#fig-scoreprops}

Scorers each missed some CDAs. CDAs with one missing score where the remaining two scores agreed were kept in the dataset, since no matter the missed third score the median would not change. Most missing scores were scored 0 by the remaining two scorers (@fig-missingscores), indicating that they were missed intentionally due to leaf damage, folding, and unclear infiltration sites, for which there is no clear CDA to score. The tolerance for skipping scores differed between scorers, with Scorer 10 missing 36 CDAs and Scorer 4 only 3.

![The frequency of missing scores by each scorer by the score collected for the same CDA by other scorers.](missing_scores.png){#fig-missingscores}

### Annotations by experiment

The agroinfiltration images were collected over many years by different researchers in the Banfield lab. They are grouped into folders according to project. The number of CDAs per agroinfiltration image differed between these project (@fig-peragrobyexperiment), reflecting differences in the number of leaves per image, the number of infiltrations per leaf, and the number of orange agroinfiltrations.

![The number of CDAs per agroinfiltration image grouped by project.](peragrobyexperiment.png){#fig-peragrobyexperiment}

### Annotations by leaf position

Anecdotal evidence exists for differences in cell death severity across leaf positions due to physiological differences in different leaf regions. The Banfield lab rotates their patterns of infiltration anti-clockwise across biological replicates to control for these effects. The annotations collected showed a decrease in mean cell death severity in leaf positions closer to the stem (@fig-leafpositionscore). This interpretation assumes that the rotation of infiltration patterns evenly distributes control experiments (expected score 0) across the leaf positions.

![Mean severity score by leaf position. Leaves varied in the number of infiltration sites, but the majority (99.0%) had 5, 6, or 8 infiltrations.](meanscorebypos.png){#fig-leafpositionscore}

## Scoring was inconsistent between scorers.

The cell death severity scores collected for a CDA often disagreed. Across the total dataset, 49.4% of CDAs had agreeing scores for all scorers. The majority of these were 0s which were both most common and by far the most consistently scored. Amongst non-zero score classes, only 23.2% of CDAs had agreeing score for all scorers (@fig-confidentscores). This provides a challenge for deep learning models, which require confidently and consistently labelled training images to learn from.

![Frequency of CDAs given 3 agreeing scores vs at least 1 disagreeing score, grouped by median score.](stackedbar.png){#fig-confidentscores}

### Average percentage agreement between scorers

I tallied all possible score comparisons across all CDAs to calculate the overall percentage agreement between scorers. If you pick any CDA at random, and pick two random scores from that CDA, the chance that they will agree is 64.2%.

0s made up a large proportion of the dataset and are much more consistently scored than other scores. This may be because the 0 class is more clearly defined as an absence of cell death whilst the differences between non-zero scores are more open to interpretation. Deep learning models require normalized class sizes, meaning the large positive contributions made by the 0s to metrics of agreement will shrink as their number is reduced to that of the smallest class, the 1s, which make up only 6.7% of the dataset. With CDAs of median score 0 removed, the percentage agreement across all pairs of scores decreases to 44.1%.

To understand the impact of the scorers' score contributions to the overall scoring agreement, I calculated the reduction in overall scoring agreement after removing the scores of each scorer in turn (@tbl-removescorer). This involved first replacing the scores with missing values, and then, if for a given CDA only one score remained or the remaining two scores disagreed, the CDA was excluded from the dataset. This second step resulted in the removal of more disagreeing scores, which is why the majority of agreement percentages increased after removing a scorer. The largest improvement in agreement was seen when removing the scores of Scorer 10 (5.49% increase). Scorer 7 was the only scorer for whom percentage agreement worsened upon removal (0.20% decrease).

| Scorer Removed | Remaining CDA Count | Overall Agreement |
|----------------|---------------------|-------------------|
| Original       | 6336                | 64.25             |
| 1              | 5978                | 64.37             |
| 2              | 5436                | 68.66             |
| 3              | 5565                | 67.56             |
| 4              | 5546                | 67.64             |
| 5              | 6066                | 67.16             |
| 6              | 5559                | 67.54             |
| 7              | 6018                | 64.05             |
| 8              | 5449                | 68.52             |
| 9              | 5446                | 68.42             |
| 10             | 5592                | 69.74             |

: Remaining CDA count and overall agreement after removing the scores of each scorer. {#tbl-removescorer}

### Agreement between scorer pair combinations

For each pair combination of scorers, I calculated a percentage scoring agreement from the CDAs scored by both scorers (@fig-pairwiseagree). Agreement varied between scoring pairs. Many pairs agreed often, with >70% agreement, whilst others agreed very rarely with <40% agreement. Scorer 10 demonstrated differences in scoring bias between scorers, agreeing with Scorer 7 in 76.6% of instances but with Scorer 8 in only 38.9% of instances. Removing CDAs of median score 0 results in a decrease of pairwise scorer agreements by roughly 20% across the board, reaching as low as 16.1% between Scorer 5 and Scorer 6 (@fig-pairwisenozero).

![Percentage scoring agreement for each pair combination of scorers](pairwiseagree_norm.png){#fig-pairwiseagree}

![Percentage scoring agreement for each pair combination of scores (with CDAs of median score 0 removed)](pairwiseagreeno0_norm.png){#fig-pairwisenozero}

In addition to the overall percentage agreement between scorer pairs, plotting a heatmap of scores for each scorer pair shows scoring trends (@fig-scoringbiases). For example, we can see that Scorer 5 typically scored higher than other scorers, whilst Scorer 4 tended to score lower. This also shows infrequent cases of large scoring disagreements, such as between Scorer 4 and Scorer 8, where Scorer 4 gave a 0, and Scorer 8 gave a 6. This indicates a scoring error has been made. These scores could be removed, but they make up a tiny proportion of the dataset and are unlikely to have a major effect on the model's performance

![Heatmap of scores collected for each pair of scorers on the same set of CDAs. CDAs of median score 0, which were much more frequent, have been removed for visual clarity.](pair_patterns_no0.png){#fig-scoringbiases}

### Metrics of model performance

The deep learning models were trained on the median score for each CDA, so their accuracy is measured against the median. The models aren't expected to achieve a 100% validation accuracy. Instead, the goal is for their performance to match that of humans.

We have the average percentage agreement with the median score by the model (current best = 65.3%). I calculated the same metric for the human scorers and directly compare it with the model. After normalising the class sizes, the average percentage agreement with the median across the human scorers was 73.2%, and within +-1 score either side of the median it was 96.8%. These values varied by scorer (@tbl-scorermedianagree). This metric may be inflated, since it is comparing scores collected against their own median.

| Scorer  | Agreement % with median score | Agreement % within +-1 of median score |
|------------------|------------------------|------------------------------|
| 1       | 73.3                          | 98.7                                   |
| 2       | 79.1                          | 98.7                                   |
| 3       | 75.6                          | 98.8                                   |
| 4       | 71.8                          | 96.5                                   |
| 5       | 48.1                          | 87.0                                   |
| 6       | 79.1                          | 98.6                                   |
| 7       | 76.6                          | 98.4                                   |
| 8       | 74.7                          | 98.1                                   |
| 9       | 75.5                          | 94.8                                   |
| 10      | 67.2                          | 93.4                                   |
| Average | 73.2                          | 96.6                                   |

: Agreement percentage of each scorer with the median score. {#tbl-scorermedianagree}

I took 10,000 samples of 500 random score pairs of the same CDA. For each sample I found the percentage agreement and the mean absolute error. I built distributions from these sampled values, and found the probability that the equivalent metric of model performance would exist within those distributions. For both the percentage agreement (p-value < 0.001)(@fig-percentagreedist) and mean absolute error (p-value = 0.002) (@fig-meanerrordist), the model performance was significantly worse than that of humans.

![Distribution of sampled percentage agreements, with red dotted line at the best model performance.](percentagreedist.png){#fig-percentagreedist}

![Distribution of sampled mean absolute errors, with red dotted line at the best model performance.](meanerrordist.png){#fig-meanerrordist}

Another method of comparing human and model performance is to see how often the model agrees with any human score of the same CDA and compare that to the same statistic for humans. We saw previously that for humans this statistic was 64.2%, but for model comparison I need to calculate an equivalent statistic for the test image dataset that the model performance was assessed on. From 560 test images, I took 10,000 samples of 100 images, calculated a) how often the model agreed with any of the human scores and b) how often the human scores agreed amongst themselves. Across these samples, the average model agreement was 57.5%, and the average human agreement was 54.0%, indicating that this test subset of the data contained a higher proportion of disagreeing scores than the rest of the dataset (@fig-matchprobhists). A t-test between the two distributions showed a significant difference in means (p < 0.001, T=71.3), and an agreement of 54.0% of lower is only found in 15.3% of cases in the model-human agreement distribution.

![Distributions of average model vs all human and all human vs all human scoring agreement in samples of size 100 (n=10,000).](modelvhuman_allcomparisons.png){#fig-matchprobhists}

However, like the human vs median metric was biased towards human performance, since it involved comparing scores against their own median, this model vs all human metric is biased in that the model has 3 potential comparisons whilst the humans only have 2.

## These scoring inconsistencies were not due to biases introduced during image assignment

The number of scores collected by each scorer matched expectations. In part A of the dataset there were some difference in scoring frequencies as a result of the orange CDAs being ignored. but in part B of the dataset all scorers recorded roughly the same number of annotations.

### CDAs scored per scorer pair combination

The number of scores collected by each pair should also follow a predictable pattern, with an expected count per pair of (2 / number of scorers \* total CDA count). However, this was not the case (@fig-pairscorefreq). We didn't see this pattern, and many pairs appeared to score far fewer CDAs than expected, despite there being no missing scores. **Why is this the case?**

::: {#fig-pairscorefreq layout-nrow="2"}
![Part A](pairscorefreq1.png){#fig-pairfreq1}

![PartB](pairscorefreq2.png){#fig-pairfreq2}

Scoring frequencies per pair combination. Red dotted line shows expected value.
:::

### Actual vs expected annotations collected per image

I plotted the number of annotations collected per image against the expected count calculated when originally distributing the images (@fig-actvsexp). For most images not containing orange CDAs, the actual count was equal to or close to the estimated count, with the exception of a couple of M1R5_M1APB_D\_scoring images. The projects containing orange CDAs, namely "Fig2_leaf_images" and "Piik (DeltaHMA)"", both showed fewer actual annotations per image than originally estimated. This makes sense given the orange CDAs were ignored. It also shows a pttern whereby the actual number was roughly 2/3, 1/2, or 1/3 of the expected number (60, 45, or 30), which would be expected with 2, 3, or 4 orange CDAs per leaf.

![Expected vs actual number of annotations collected per agroinfiltration image, coloured by project](expectedvsactual.png){#fig-actvsexp}

This shows us that although some pairs of scorers collected fewer CDAs than expected, this wasn't because they missed scores. This was also confirmed when I manually checked each agroinfiltration image to ensure the coordinate boxes were correctly matched to the positional metadata (row, column, position).

### Distribution of images by project amongst scorers

Agroinfiltration images were randomly assigned amongst the scores. The number of images of each project were evenly distributed amongst scorers (@fig-experimentalloc). Where Scorers 1, 5, and 7 have 0 assigned agroinfiltration images for some projects it is because they did not annotate that part of the dataset.

![Distribution of images by project amongst scorers.](experimentalloc.png){#fig-experimentalloc}

\newpage

## Inconsistencies may instead be due different opinions on the varied images and how they relate to the scoring key.

Looking at example CDA images (@fig-examplecdas), we can see features within classes which introduce variation, such as lighting conditions, veins, damage, and black background regions. It is clear to the eye the differences between distant score classes, but sometimes more challenging to distinguish between images of adjacent classes.

![Examples of CDAs annotated, grouped into columns by median score.](cdaexamples.png){#fig-examplecdas}

The scoring key (@fig-scoringkey) contains just a single example CDA for each class. The variation across the image dataset means that sometimes the CDAs to be scored look very different to anything in the scoring key. This would leave the score up to the interpretation of the individual scorer. In this way, differences of scoring opinion could introduce the scoring inconsistencies that were seen in the dataset.

![Scoring key used to collect image annotations.](lesion_score_key.jpg){#fig-scoringkey}

### PCA

I applied PCA dimensionality reduction to the raw pixel values of the 64x64-pixel CDA images and coloured by the median score (@fig-pixelpca). The first 2 PCs explain almost half (47.9%) of the variation in the images, which is good considering the reduction from 12,288 dimensions (64x64x3). The trend seen in the example CDA images was repeated here. Distant scores can be distinguished on the plot, and there is a trend of increasing PC1 and decreasing PC2 as the median score increases. However, it is not possible to draw class boundaries between adjacent score classes.

![PCA of CDA image raw pixel values coloured by median score.](pixelpca.png){#fig-pixelpca}

A contributing factor to these class overlaps could be the continuous nature of the underlying cell death severity trait, which we have grouped into score classes for convenience. Although the classes are categorical, they are nominal, meaning that the true boundary of one class directly abutts the next. This means that any scoring inconsistencies will overlap with the adjacent class.

\newpage

## Non-DL clustering methods are unable to define accurate class boundaries

### K-Means and Hierarchical Clustering

Overlapping variation between classes makes it challenging for non-DL clustering methods to find groupings in the data that match the given scores. K-Means Clustering was applied to the CDA image pixel values (@fig-kmeanspca). It failed due to the assumption of spherical clusters, which the earlier PCA (@fig-pixelpca) showed to be unlikely. Hierarchical clustering was also attempted but failed for the same reason.

![PCA of CDA images by pixel value coloured by K-Means cluster](kmeanspca.png){#fig-kmeanspca}

### DBSCAN

DBSCAN is a density-based clustering method which allows for non-uniform cluster shapes. Since KMeans and Hierarchical clustering failed due to their assumption of spherical classes, we reasoned that DBSCAN may be free of that limitation and therefore perform better. However, DBSCAN also failed due to the fact that all images in the dataset cluster together (@fig-dbscanpca). Given a minimum class size of 50 points, there was only ever 1 class, with the remainder marked as noise. The size of the class relative to the noise just grew as the maximum permitted distance between points of the same class was increased, with no change to the number of predicted classes.

![PCA of CDA images by pixel value coloured by DBSCAN class assignments. -1 means noise.](dbscanpca.png){#fig-dbscanpca}

### Kohonen Mapping

Kohonen mapping, also known as self-organising maps, were also implemented. This is an unsupervised learning method that assigns images to "nodes" in a neural network, which can be thought of as classes. These nodes "win" images based on Euclidian distance in an iterative process. I trained Kohonen maps with a vertical shape of (7, 1) in an attempt to impose ordinality on the node classes. In the PCA of pixel values, we saw that score typically increased with increasing PC1 and decreasing PC2.

I attempted to impose order on the nodes by initializing higher node weights for higher classes. I trained 150 Kohonen maps with different sets of input parameters (learning rate, duration, random/ordered weight initialization, and sigma (how much is one node affected by updates to its neighbour)). Given the attempt to order the classes, I chose as the best model that whose class labels best matched the median score labels collected by humans scorers. The best, with input parameters sigma=2, learning_rate=0.7, duration=3500, and initialization="ordered", achieved 29.5% accuracy (@fig-kohonenpca), (@fig-kohonenclasses).

![PCA of CDA images by pixel value coloured by Kohonen Map class assignments.](kohonenpca.png){#fig-kohonenpca}

![Heatmap of score distributions assigned to each Kohonen Map class.](kohonenclasses.png){#fig-kohonenclasses}

I also trained 300 Kohonen maps with a difference performance metric. This time, for each node in a given model, I mapped the images "won" by the node to their median score label, then calculated the variance of those labels. I summed these variances across all nodes for the model. I then found the model with the lowest sum of median score variances within its nodes (variance = 1.19, sigma=0.5, learning_rate=0.1, duration=10,000, initialization=random). However, this model only used 5 of the 7 available nodes, and three of the remaining nodes were primarily 0s, one mostly 5s and 6s, and the remaining one mostly 3-5s but also many 0s.

Kohonen maps appear to show more varied class assignments than other methods, but are still unable to find clusters in the data that correspond to score classes.

\newpage

## Dataset learnability

Deep learning models learn from patterns in the data. If annotations are inconsistent, this can confuse the model during training, leading to poor performance. Using the median as the annotation label for training may have mitigated some of the variation seen between individual scorers, but we still saw overlapping variation between median score classes.

The models trained so far achieved a maximum validation accuracy of 65.4% (+-1=96.8%) (@tbl-modelaccuracies). For each new model type, a new training, validation, and test split are generated, meaning it's no single subset of the image dataset that is limiting the model's performance. The dataset as a whole is limited in its learnability.

| Model type                    | Agreement with median % | +-1 Agreement with median % |
|-----------------------------------|-------------------|-------------------|
| Human average                 | 73.14                   | 96.79                       |
| Mixed augmented 7000          | 65.36                   | 96.79                       |
| Ensemble softmax              | 64.29                   | 96.54                       |
| Original dataset              | 62.17                   | 96.90                       |
| Geometrically augmented 700   | 61.65                   | 96.12                       |
| Confident dataset             | 61.18                   | 94.78                       |
| Transfer learning MobileNetV2 | 55.20                   | 92.52                       |

: Model performances ranked by accuracy {#tbl-modelaccuracies}

The pattern of human scoring is reflected in the model (@fig-bestcm). The model is within +-1 of the median score almost always, but often struggles to classify between images of adjacent score classes.

![The confusion matrix comparing model scores and human predictions from the current best performing model](bestcm.png){#fig-bestcm}

The model applies rigid learned rules when classifying CDA images. It objectively classifies new images based on what it's seen before in training. For CDAs in less common or ambiguous settings, the model does not have the wider contextual understanding that humans do. Model accuracy is defined by comparing to human scorers, which I've shown to be consistent. The rigidity of the classification rules learned by the model may in fact may provide a more consistent scoring method than humans, causing disagreements with less consistent human scores.

\newpage

## Next steps to improve model

Removing the scores of some scorers increased the average pairwise scoring agreement. I will train deep learning models on datasets excluding each scorer to see if increased scoring agreement translates to increased model performance.

There were some erroneous annotations where scores collected for the same CDA differed by 3 or more classes. These will be excluded from the dataset.

The median score doesn't capture score variation for each CDA. I will design a new system of labels to incorporate this, perhaps negatively weighting images with greater score variation, or taking a mean score and building a regression model.

The 0-6 scoring system was introduced based on a specific need for an experiment, but may not be the most effective way of scoring the data. Changing the number of classes or choosing a new label may help the model more clearly define boundaries between score classes. Any new scoring system should balance model performance with biological relevance, since for example a presence/absence model would perform very well but not meet the task requirements.

It is possible that the model performs poorly on specific edge cases or certain image types. Adversarial methods will help identify these images, allowing for further targetted model training.

I may change the metric used to define model success. The human average agreement of the median is measuring success against itself and may therefore be an overinflated estimate of human performance, which is why the model is unable to achieve it. It may be better to instead treat the model as another scorer and look at agreement against all scores for the given CDA rather than only the median. This could coincide with a model where all three scores are incorporated into model training and model performance is defined by comparing against all scores.
